final_text: It was not without a certain wild pleasure that I ran before the wind, delivering my troubled mind to the boundless storm thundering through space. Coming down the laurel walk, I faced the wreck of the chestnut tree. It stood black and torn apart, its trunk split down the centre, gaping ghastly. The two halves were not broken from each other, for the firm base and strong roots kept them joined below. But the shared life was destroyed — the sap could flow no more. Their great boughs on each side were dead, and next winter's storms would surely bring one or both crashing to earth. Yet for now, they could still be called one tree — a ruin, but a complete ruin.

final_text: "All day yesterday I was very busy and very happy in my constant activity. I am not, as you seem to think, troubled by any haunting fears about the new life ahead of me, and so on. I think it a glorious thing to have the hope of living with you, because I love you. No, sir, don't caress me now — let me talk undisturbed. Yesterday I trusted in Providence, and believed that events were working together for your good and mine. It was a fine day, if you recall — the calm air and sky forbade worries about your safety or comfort on your journey. I walked a little while on the pavement after tea, thinking of you, and I pictured you so near me in my imagination that I scarcely missed your actual presence. I thought of the life that lay before me — your life, sir — an existence wider and more stirring than my own: as much more so as the depths of the ocean to which a brook runs are wider than the shallows of its own narrow channel. I wondered why moralists call this world a dreary wilderness. For me it blossomed like a rose. Just at sunset, the air turned cold and the sky cloudy. I went in. Sophie called me upstairs to look at my wedding dress, which they had just brought, and under it in the box I found your present — the veil which, in your princely extravagance, you had sent for from London, resolved, I suppose, since I would not have jewels, to trick me into accepting something equally costly. I smiled as I unfolded it, and planned how I would tease you about your aristocratic tastes and your efforts to disguise your common-born bride in the trappings of a noblewoman. I thought how I would carry down to you the square of plain lace I had prepared myself as a covering for my lowly head, and ask if that was not good enough for a woman who could bring her husband neither fortune, beauty, nor connections. I saw plainly how you would look, and heard your impetuous, republican answers and your proud dismissal of any need on your part to add to your wealth or raise your standing by marrying either a purse or a title."

final_text: "No, no, sir. Besides the delicacy and richness of the fabric, I found nothing but Fairfax Rochester's pride. And that did not frighten me, because I am used to seeing that particular demon. But, sir, as it grew dark, the wind rose. It blew yesterday evening, not as it blows now — wild and high — but 'with a sullen, moaning sound,' far more eerie. I wished you were home. I came into this room, and the sight of the empty chair and fireless hearth chilled me. For some time after I went to bed, I could not sleep. A sense of anxious excitement plagued me. The rising gale seemed to muffle some mournful under-sound. Whether it came from inside the house or outside I could not at first tell, but it returned, faint yet doleful, at every pause in the wind. At last I made out it must be some dog howling in the distance. I was glad when it stopped. When I fell asleep, I continued in dreams the idea of a dark and gusty night. I continued also the wish to be with you, and I felt a strange, sorrowful awareness of some barrier separating us. During all my first sleep, I was following the twists of an unknown road. Total darkness surrounded me. Rain pelted me. I was burdened with a little child — a very small creature, too young and weak to walk, which shivered in my cold arms and wailed miserably in my ear. I thought, sir, that you were on the road far ahead of me, and I strained every nerve to overtake you, and made effort upon effort to call your name and beg you to stop — but my movements were shackled, and my voice kept dying away, wordless. While you, I felt, drew farther and farther away with every moment."

final_text: "Well," he said, after some minutes' silence, "it is strange, but that sentence has pierced my heart painfully. Why? I think because you said it with such earnest, religious intensity, and because your upward gaze at me now is the very essence of faith, truth, and devotion. It is too much as if some spirit were near me. Look wicked, Jane — as you know well how to look. Show me one of your wild, shy, teasing smiles. Tell me you hate me — tease me, provoke me. Do anything but move me. I would rather be angered than saddened."

The fiery eyes glared at me — she thrust the candle close to my face and snuffed it out before my eyes. I was aware her lurid face blazed over mine, and I lost consciousness. For the second time in my life — only the second time — I fainted from sheer terror."

final_text: Mr. Rochester, on hearing the name, clenched his teeth. He experienced, too, a sort of violent, convulsive tremor. Near to him as I was, I felt the spasm of fury or despair run through his body. The second stranger, who had until then lingered in the background, now drew near. A pale face looked over the solicitor's shoulder — yes, it was Mason himself. Mr. Rochester turned and glared at him. His eye, as I have often said, was a dark eye. It had now a tawny, even bloody light in its depth. His face flushed — his olive cheek and pale forehead received a glow as from a spreading, rising fire in his heart. He stirred, lifted his strong arm — he could have struck Mason, dashed him to the church floor, knocked the breath from his body with one ruthless blow — but Mason shrank away and cried faintly, "Good God!" Contempt fell cold on Mr. Rochester — his passion died as if a blight had withered it. He only asked — "What have you to say?"

The madwoman sprang and seized his throat savagely, sinking her teeth into his cheek. They struggled. She was a big woman, nearly as tall as her husband, and heavy besides. She showed a man's strength in the fight — more than once she almost throttled him, athletic as he was. He could have brought her down with a single well-placed blow, but he would not strike. He would only wrestle. At last he mastered her arms. Grace Poole gave him a cord, and he tied them behind her. With more rope, which was near at hand, he bound her to a chair. The task was performed amid the fiercest screams and the most violent struggles. Mr. Rochester then turned to the onlookers. He looked at them with a smile both bitter and desolate.

And this is what I wished to have" — laying his hand on my shoulder — "this young girl, who stands so grave and quiet at the mouth of hell, looking calmly at the antics of a demon. I wanted her just as a change of diet after that fierce stew. Wood and Briggs, look at the difference! Compare these clear eyes with the red ones over there — this face with that mask — this figure with that bulk. Then judge me, priest of the gospel and man of the law, and remember that with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged! Off with you now. I must lock up my prize."

final_text: "Mr. Mason does. Mr. Eyre has been the Funchal correspondent of his firm for some years. When your uncle received your letter mentioning the planned union between yourself and Mr. Rochester, Mr. Mason, who was staying in Madeira to restore his health on his way back to Jamaica, happened to be with him. Mr. Eyre mentioned the news, for he knew that my client here was acquainted with a gentleman named Rochester. Mr. Mason, as astonished and distressed as you may imagine, revealed the true state of affairs. Your uncle, I am sorry to say, is now on his sickbed — from which, considering the nature of his disease — a wasting decline — and the stage it has reached, it is unlikely he will ever rise. He could not then hurry to England himself to rescue you from the trap you had fallen into, but he begged Mr. Mason to lose no time in taking steps to prevent the fraudulent marriage. He referred him to me for help. I acted with all speed, and am thankful I was not too late — as you, no doubt, must be also. Were I not morally certain that your uncle will be dead before you reach Madeira, I would advise you to accompany Mr. Mason back. But as it is, I think you had better remain in England until you can hear further, either from or of Mr. Eyre. Have we anything else to stay for?" he asked of Mr. Mason.

final_text: I heard him go as I stood at the half-open door of my own room, to which I had now retreated. The house emptied, I shut myself in, fastened the bolt so that no one might intrude, and proceeded — not to weep, not to mourn (I was yet too calm for that) — but mechanically to take off the wedding dress and replace it with the plain gown I had worn yesterday, as I thought, for the last time. I then sat down. I felt weak and tired. I leaned my arms on the table and my head dropped onto them. And now I thought. Until now I had only heard, seen, moved — followed up and down where I was led or dragged — watched event rush on event, revelation open beyond revelation. But now, I thought.

final_text: Jane Eyre, who had been a passionate, expectant woman — almost a bride — was a cold, solitary girl again. Her life was pale. Her prospects were desolate. A Christmas frost had come at midsummer. A white December storm had whirled over June. Ice glazed the ripe apples. Drifts crushed the blooming roses. On hayfield and cornfield lay a frozen shroud. Lanes which last night blushed full of flowers were today pathless with untrodden snow. And the woods, which twelve hours ago waved leafy and fragrant as tropical groves, now spread waste, wild, and white as pine forests in wintry Norway. My hopes were all dead — struck with a subtle doom, such as, in one night, fell on all the firstborn in the land of Egypt. I looked at my cherished wishes, yesterday so blooming and bright. They lay stark, cold, livid corpses that could never revive. I looked at my love — that feeling which was my master's, which he had created. It shivered in my heart like a suffering child in a cold cradle. Sickness and anguish had seized it. It could not seek Mr. Rochester's arms — it could not draw warmth from his breast. Oh, never more could it turn to him, for faith was shattered — trust was destroyed! Mr. Rochester was not to me what he had been, for he was not what I had thought him. I would not call him wicked. I would not say he had betrayed me. But the quality of untarnished truth was gone from my idea of him, and from his presence I must go. That I saw clearly. When — how — where, I could not yet determine. But he himself, I had no doubt, would hurry me from Thornfield. Real affection, it seemed, he could not have for me. It had been only fitful passion — that was thwarted, and he would want me no more. I should fear even to cross his path now. My very sight must be hateful to him. Oh, how blind my eyes had been! How weak my conduct!

Giving myself up, limp and without effort, I seemed to have lain down in the dried-up bed of a great river. I heard a flood unleashed in remote mountains and felt the torrent coming. To rise I had no will. To flee I had no strength. I lay faint, longing to be dead. One idea only still throbbed with life inside me — a memory of God. It stirred a wordless prayer.
